**🎯 Today's Goal:**
Your child will memorize the "price" of every chess piece and understand that points are used to measure an army's strength, but having the most points does not mean you win the game.

**✅ Lesson Success Criteria:**
- The child can accurately state the value of the Pawn, Knight, Bishop, Rook, and Queen.
- The child understands the King has no point value (he is priceless).
- The child can add the points of a small group of pieces (e.g., Rook + Pawn = 6).

*(Purpose: "Can I teach this today?" A quick summary for busy parents.)*

parent_reference.heading: 2. Definition
parent_reference.content: In chess, each piece is assigned a point value based on how powerful it is. The Pawn is worth 1, the Knight and Bishop are 3, the Rook is 5, and the Queen is 9. The King cannot be captured, so he is worth infinity (or priceless). These points do not determine who wins the game. Instead, they are a mathematical tool to help players understand if they are making a fair trade when pieces capture each other.

parent_reference.heading: 3. Why It Matters
parent_reference.content: Children naturally want to capture pieces, but without knowing their values, they might happily let their Queen be captured just to take an enemy Pawn! Teaching piece values gives the child a concrete, mathematical way to measure danger and value.

parent_reference.heading: 4. Before You Teach (Graph)
parent_reference.content:
- **Requires:** TOP-104 through TOP-109 (Movement Layer)
- **Unlocks:** TOP-101 (Exchanges & Trades), TOP-016 (Game Phases)

parent_reference.heading: 5. Parent Understands
parent_reference.content:
In many sports, points determine the winner. In chess, points are an illusion. A player can have 20 more points than their opponent and still lose the game via checkmate on the next turn. 
However, points are an essential measuring stick. 
The scale is built around the pawn. 
- Pawn = 1
- Knight / Bishop = 3 (A minor piece is worth about 3 pawns).
- Rook = 5 (A Rook is worth a minor piece plus 2 pawns).
- Queen = 9 (The Queen is almost as strong as two Rooks!).
- King = Priceless.

parent_reference.heading: 6. How to Teach It
parent_reference.content:
1. **The Chess Store:** Lay out one of each White piece in front of your child. Tell them, "Welcome to the Chess Store! Every piece costs a certain number of gold coins."
2. **The Pawn:** "The Pawn is the smallest soldier. He costs 1 gold coin."
3. **The Twins:** "The Knight and the Bishop are stronger. They cost 3 gold coins each."
4. **The Heavy Pieces:** "The Rook is a big castle. It costs 5 coins. The Queen is the superhero. She costs 9 coins!"
5. **The King:** "How much does the King cost? You can't buy the King! If you lose the King, you lose the kingdom. He is priceless!"
6. **The Pop Quiz:** Point to pieces randomly and have the child shout out the price.

parent_reference.heading: 7. Teaching Story / Analogy / Memory Hint
parent_reference.content:
**The Gold Coin Bank:** 
Imagine you have a big bag of gold coins. 
If you want to hire a little foot-soldier (Pawn), you pay 1 coin. 
If you want to hire a brave guy on a horse (Knight) or a magic wizard (Bishop), you pay 3 coins. 
If you want to build a giant rolling castle tower (Rook), you pay 5 coins. 
If you want to hire the flying superhero (Queen), it costs 9 whole coins! 
But the King? The King *owns* all the gold! You can't buy him!

parent_reference.heading: 8. Did You Know? 🎓
parent_reference.content: Because the Knight and the Bishop are both worth 3 points, they are usually considered perfectly equal. However, depending on the shape of the pawn walls on the board, sometimes the horse is better, and sometimes the wizard is better!

parent_reference.heading: 9. Board Diagram 1 — Basic Concept
parent_reference.content:
![DGM-014-01: A chart showing the Pawn (1), Knight (3), Bishop (3), Rook (5), Queen (9), and King (Infinity).](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-014/DGM-014-01.svg)
*The standard point values for the chess army.*

parent_reference.heading: 10. How It Works
parent_reference.content: Points are just a way to do math in your head before you decide to capture. If you capture a 3-point piece, but the enemy immediately captures your 9-point Queen, you just lost 6 points of power! We use these numbers to avoid making bad deals.

parent_reference.heading: 11. Board Diagram 2 — Practical Example
parent_reference.content:
![DGM-014-02: One Queen on the left side of the board. Nine Pawns lined up on the right side.](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-014/DGM-014-02.svg)
*A Queen is worth 9 points. That means she is as strong as 9 pawns working together!*

parent_reference.heading: 12. Real Game Example
parent_reference.content:
![DGM-014-03: A White Rook (5) and a Black Knight (3) and two Black Pawns (1+1).](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-014/DGM-014-03.svg)
*A Rook is worth 5 points. If you trade your Rook to capture a Knight and two Pawns, it is a perfectly fair deal (5 = 3 + 1 + 1).*

parent_reference.heading: 13. Common Mistakes
parent_reference.content:
- **Thinking points win the game:** Children often count their captured pieces at the side of the board and say, "I'm winning by 4 points!" Remind them that checkmate ends the game, not the score.
- **Forgetting the King:** When asked how much the King is worth, kids will guess "10" or "100". 

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> If a child says the King is worth 10, ask them: "Would you trade your King to capture a Queen and a Pawn (9+1 = 10)?" They will quickly realize that losing the King loses the game, so he cannot have a number!

parent_reference.heading: 14. Teaching Notes
parent_reference.content:
This is a math lesson disguised as a chess lesson. For a 6-year-old, adding 5 + 3 might require finger counting. Be extremely patient. The goal is the chess concept, not testing their arithmetic speed. 

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> Do not introduce the concept of "good trades" and "bad trades" yet. Right now, just focus on rote memorization of the values. We will learn how to use these numbers in the "Exchanges" lesson.

parent_reference.heading: 15. Parent FAQ
parent_reference.content:
**Q: I heard some people say the Bishop is worth 3.5 points. Is that true?**
A: Advanced chess computers do value the Bishop slightly higher than the Knight (around 3.15 to 3.5). But for human beginners, they are both exactly 3. Keep it simple!

**Q: Do we keep score during the game?**
A: It is highly recommended NOT to keep a running score during the game. It distracts the child from looking at the board. The points only matter right before a capture happens.

parent_reference.heading: 16. Practice Together
parent_reference.content:
**The Math Matcher:**
Take all the pieces off the board. You (the parent) put down a piece (e.g., a Rook). The child must build a "team" of pieces that equals exactly the same number of points (e.g., a Bishop and two Pawns, or 5 Pawns). Take turns challenging each other with different pieces.

parent_reference.heading: 17. Coach Challenge ⭐
parent_reference.content:
**The Greedy Goblin:**
Set up a White Queen on `d4`. Place a Black Pawn on `a7`, a Black Knight on `h8`, and a Black Rook on `d1`. 
Tell your child: "You are a Greedy Goblin! You want to steal the most expensive treasure in one turn."
Have them identify the point values of the three targets (1, 3, and 5). 
Then, have them move the Queen to capture the most valuable piece! (The Rook!).

parent_reference.heading: 18. Try It Yourself
parent_reference.content:
### 🟢 Recognition (Easy)
![DGM-014-04: A picture of a Bishop, a Rook, and a Queen.](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-014/DGM-014-04.svg)
**Question:** Which piece is worth 5 points?
**Answer:** The Rook! (The Castle).

### 🟡 Application (Medium)
![DGM-014-05: White has two Knights (3+3). Black has one Rook (5).](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-014/DGM-014-05.svg)
**Question:** White has two horses. Black has one castle. Who has more points?
**Answer:** White! Two Knights = 6 points. One Rook = 5 points.

### 🔴 Challenge (Hard)
![DGM-014-06: White Queen on c3. Black Pawn on c4 (protected by a Black Rook on c8).](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-014/DGM-014-06.svg)
**Question:** The White Queen wants to capture the Black Pawn. If she does, the Black Rook will capture her back! Is trading a Queen (9) for a Pawn (1) a good idea?
**Answer:** No! You would win 1 point, but lose 9 points! That is a terrible deal at the Chess Store!

parent_reference.heading: 19. Continue Learning
parent_reference.content: - **Lichess Practice:** [Piece Values](https://lichess.org/learn#/7) (Interactive drills).

parent_reference.heading: 20. Related Topics
parent_reference.content:
- **Prerequisites:** TOP-109 Pawn Movement
- **Next Steps:** TOP-015 Initial Position, TOP-101 Exchanges & Trades

parent_reference.heading: 21. Parent Confidence Check ✅
parent_reference.content:
- [ ] Can my child name the value of all 5 combat pieces?
- [ ] Does my child understand the King is priceless?
- [ ] Did we play the "Math Matcher" game?
- [ ] Does my child understand that points don't win the game?

teach_slides.title: The Chess Store
teach_slides.text: Learn what each chess piece costs in gold coins.
teach_slides.parent_prompt: Open the Chess Store and explain that each piece has a standard coin value.

teach_slides.title: The value lineup
teach_slides.text: Pawn 1 Knight 3 Bishop 3 Rook 5 Queen 9; the King is priceless.
teach_slides.parent_prompt: Point to each piece while the child repeats its value.

teach_slides.title: Nine Pawns and one Queen
teach_slides.text: Nine one-point Pawns total the same number of points as one Queen.
teach_slides.parent_prompt: Count the nine Pawns and compare their total with the Queen.
teach_slides.position_title: One Queen compared with nine Pawns
teach_slides.diagram_alt: One Queen compared with nine Pawns

teach_slides.title: Two ways to make five
teach_slides.text: A Knight and two Pawns total five points the same number as a Rook.
teach_slides.parent_prompt: Add three plus one plus one without discussing whether to exchange the pieces.

teach_slides.title: Find five points
teach_slides.text: Which piece is worth five points?
teach_slides.parent_prompt: Ask which displayed piece is worth five points before revealing the answer.

teach_slides.title: Six or five
teach_slides.text: Do two Knights or one Rook have more points?
teach_slides.parent_prompt: Let the child total both groups and say which has more points.
teach_slides.reveal: Two Knights total 6 points; one Rook is 5.

teach_slides.diagram_alt: Two Knights compared with one Rook

teach_slides.text: Name the values and explain why points do not win the game.
teach_slides.parent_prompt: Check recall small-group addition and the meaning of priceless.

memory_phrase: One, three, three, five, nine; the King is priceless.

slides.text: Learn what each chess piece costs in gold coins.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.text:
- **Topic**: Piece Values
- **Difficulty**: Beginner
- **Typical age**: 6+
- **Estimated teaching time**: 15 min
- **Piece/concept type**: Rule
- **Prerequisites**: All Movement Layer Topics (TOP-104 to TOP-109)

**🎯 Today's Goal:**
Your child will memorize the "price" of every chess piece and understand that points are used to measure an army's strength, but having the most points does not mean you win the game.

**✅ Lesson Success Criteria:**
- The child can accurately state the value of the Pawn, Knight, Bishop, Rook, and Queen.
- The child understands the King has no point value (he is priceless).
- The child can add the points of a small group of pieces (e.g., Rook + Pawn = 6).

*(Purpose: "Can I teach this today?" A quick summary for busy parents.)*

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: In chess, each piece is assigned a point value based on how powerful it is. The Pawn is worth 1, the Knight and Bishop are 3, the Rook is 5, and the Queen is 9. The King cannot be captured, so he is worth infinity (or priceless). These points do not determine who wins the game. Instead, they are a mathematical tool to help players understand if they are making a fair trade when pieces capture each other.

sections.title: Why It Matters
sections.text: Children naturally want to capture pieces, but without knowing their values, they might happily let their Queen be captured just to take an enemy Pawn! Teaching piece values gives the child a concrete, mathematical way to measure danger and value.

sections.title: Before You Teach (Graph)

- **Requires:** TOP-104 through TOP-109 (Movement Layer)
- **Unlocks:** TOP-101 (Exchanges & Trades), TOP-016 (Game Phases)

sections.title: Parent Understands
sections.text:
In many sports, points determine the winner. In chess, points are an illusion. A player can have 20 more points than their opponent and still lose the game via checkmate on the next turn. 
However, points are an essential measuring stick. 
The scale is built around the pawn. 
- Pawn = 1
- Knight / Bishop = 3 (A minor piece is worth about 3 pawns).
- Rook = 5 (A Rook is worth a minor piece plus 2 pawns).
- Queen = 9 (The Queen is almost as strong as two Rooks!).
- King = Priceless.

sections.title: How to Teach It
sections.text:
1. **The Chess Store:** Lay out one of each White piece in front of your child. Tell them, "Welcome to the Chess Store! Every piece costs a certain number of gold coins."
2. **The Pawn:** "The Pawn is the smallest soldier. He costs 1 gold coin."
3. **The Twins:** "The Knight and the Bishop are stronger. They cost 3 gold coins each."
4. **The Heavy Pieces:** "The Rook is a big castle. It costs 5 coins. The Queen is the superhero. She costs 9 coins!"
5. **The King:** "How much does the King cost? You can't buy the King! If you lose the King, you lose the kingdom. He is priceless!"
6. **The Pop Quiz:** Point to pieces randomly and have the child shout out the price.

sections.title: Teaching Story / Analogy / Memory Hint
sections.text:
**The Gold Coin Bank:** 
Imagine you have a big bag of gold coins. 
If you want to hire a little foot-soldier (Pawn), you pay 1 coin. 
If you want to hire a brave guy on a horse (Knight) or a magic wizard (Bishop), you pay 3 coins. 
If you want to build a giant rolling castle tower (Rook), you pay 5 coins. 
If you want to hire the flying superhero (Queen), it costs 9 whole coins! 
But the King? The King *owns* all the gold! You can't buy him!

sections.title: Did You Know? 🎓
sections.text: Because the Knight and the Bishop are both worth 3 points, they are usually considered perfectly equal. However, depending on the shape of the pawn walls on the board, sometimes the horse is better, and sometimes the wizard is better!

sections.title: How It Works
sections.text: Points are just a way to do math in your head before you decide to capture. If you capture a 3-point piece, but the enemy immediately captures your 9-point Queen, you just lost 6 points of power! We use these numbers to avoid making bad deals.

sections.title: Real Game Example
sections.text: *A Rook is worth 5 points. If you trade your Rook to capture a Knight and two Pawns, it is a perfectly fair deal (5 = 3 + 1 + 1).*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.text:
- **Thinking points win the game:** Children often count their captured pieces at the side of the board and say, "I'm winning by 4 points!" Remind them that checkmate ends the game, not the score.
- **Forgetting the King:** When asked how much the King is worth, kids will guess "10" or "100".

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> If a child says the King is worth 10, ask them: "Would you trade your King to capture a Queen and a Pawn (9+1 = 10)?" They will quickly realize that losing the King loses the game, so he cannot have a number!

sections.title: Teaching Notes
sections.text:
This is a math lesson disguised as a chess lesson. For a 6-year-old, adding 5 + 3 might require finger counting. Be extremely patient. The goal is the chess concept, not testing their arithmetic speed.

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> Do not introduce the concept of "good trades" and "bad trades" yet. Right now, just focus on rote memorization of the values. We will learn how to use these numbers in the "Exchanges" lesson.

sections.title: Parent FAQ
sections.text:
**Q: I heard some people say the Bishop is worth 3.5 points. Is that true?**
A: Advanced chess computers do value the Bishop slightly higher than the Knight (around 3.15 to 3.5). But for human beginners, they are both exactly 3. Keep it simple!

**Q: Do we keep score during the game?**
A: It is highly recommended NOT to keep a running score during the game. It distracts the child from looking at the board. The points only matter right before a capture happens.

sections.title: Practice Together
sections.text:
**The Math Matcher:**
Take all the pieces off the board. You (the parent) put down a piece (e.g., a Rook). The child must build a "team" of pieces that equals exactly the same number of points (e.g., a Bishop and two Pawns, or 5 Pawns). Take turns challenging each other with different pieces.

sections.title: Coach Challenge ⭐
sections.text:
**The Greedy Goblin:**
Set up a White Queen on `d4`. Place a Black Pawn on `a7`, a Black Knight on `h8`, and a Black Rook on `d1`. 
Tell your child: "You are a Greedy Goblin! You want to steal the most expensive treasure in one turn."
Have them identify the point values of the three targets (1, 3, and 5). 
Then, have them move the Queen to capture the most valuable piece! (The Rook!).

sections.title: Try It Yourself
sections.text:
### 🟢 Recognition (Easy)

**Question:** Which piece is worth 5 points?
**Answer:** The Rook! (The Castle).

### 🟡 Application (Medium)

**Question:** White has two horses. Black has one castle. Who has more points?
**Answer:** White! Two Knights = 6 points. One Rook = 5 points.

### 🔴 Challenge (Hard)

**Question:** The White Queen wants to capture the Black Pawn. If she does, the Black Rook will capture her back! Is trading a Queen (9) for a Pawn (1) a good idea?
**Answer:** No! You would win 1 point, but lose 9 points! That is a terrible deal at the Chess Store!
